subject: arcticOutpost
pitch:
Category: Diorama.
Subject: arctic research outpost.
Style: Firewatch flat colour.
reasoning:
I'm planning out a single TypeScript module for an arctic research outpost diorama in a Firewatch-style flat color aesthetic, with a static model using layered silhouettes and a warm gradient sky palette, aiming for clean, correct code without needing joints for the props.

For the diorama itself, I'm sketching the full scene: a chunky snow/ice terrain slab base, a red-orange main hut with a sloped roof, a smaller stilted lab module, radio mast, weather station gear, a snowmobile, fuel drums, flag, antenna dish, solar panels, wind turbine, sled, glowing lantern-lit windows, a footprint path, and layered mountain silhouettes with a big sunset sun disk in the background, all sized at a tabletop diorama scale around 3 x 2.4 meters. Since this is a static model, I'm confirming it's fine to skip joints entirely and just build geometry directly onto the root.

I'm keeping the palette tight within the 64-flat-color limit, using gradient paints for the Firewatch warm-to-cool vertical look, and planning the base as an extruded terrain outline with a dark rock stratum beneath the snow cap to echo that layered aesthetic.

For the snow layer, I'm building a smoothed irregular blob outline with radius variation to avoid self-intersection, stacking the rock, ice, and snow bands at increasing scale and height, and adding flattened sphere mounds for drifts before moving on to the backdrop.

I also want a backdrop panel behind the scene — a gradient sky extrude from peach near the horizon to deep purple above, positioned behind the terrain, though I'm second-guessing whether that fits the "nothing hangs above" constraint.

I'm working out the panel dimensions so it fits within the base footprint — since the base blob's rounded corners would clip a wide rectangular panel, I'm switching to a rounded rectangular base instead, roughly 3.4 across, to keep the backdrop edges contained.

I'm defining mountain ridge silhouettes as closed polylines with peaks, placed at different depths with a gradient of colors from peach to deep purple to create atmospheric perspective.

For texturing, I'll use a paint function that checks the surface position and applies snow-white coloring above a certain height while keeping the base color below. I'm layering multiple ridges with slight gaps in front of the panel, positioning them so their bases sit low enough to be hidden behind the ground's snow cap.

Now I'm working out the sun as a glowing flat circle placed just in front of the sky panel, carefully spacing the z-depths so the panel, sun, and ridges stack correctly without clipping into each other.

For the sky itself, I'm planning a vertical gradient keyed to y-position, going from a peach tone near the horizon up to a deep purple near the top, possibly quantized into bands to get that stylized Firewatch look.

For the panel I'll build an outline rect with extrude for the sky plane, and I'm considering adding tiny glowing star dots near the top with some randomness for texture. I'm also thinking about adding an aurora ribbon to give the sky more visual interest.

I'll render the aurora as an SVG texture with alpha cutout—wavy teal and mint bands layered subtly high in the sky so it doesn't clash with the sunset gradient, using a muted teal tone. Now I'm moving on to planning the outpost layout.

I need to confirm the viewer's orientation relative to the model, then set the ground elevation at 0.40 with rock, ice, and snow bands stacked beneath it. I'm sizing the main hut relative to a realistic 6x4m structure scaled down, giving it raised stilts, a roof ridge, and proportioned wall height and door size based on that scale.

Now I'm designing the hut's support structure with skid runners and stilt posts, then working out a siding paint function that adds horizontal grain lines and lighting-based shading to the walls.

Writing shading helper function...

For the house itself, I'm planning to extrude a pentagon profile (forming the gable wall shape) along the depth axis to create the whole body with walls and gable ends in one piece, then add separate rotated box slabs on top for the overhanging roof panels.

I'll add a slightly smaller white snow layer on top of each roof panel for the snowy effect, then wrap all this into a reusable gable-building helper so I can create both the main hut and a smaller second module in different Firewatch-inspired colors like teal and mustard.

For the second module, I'm considering making it a quonset-style hut with a half-cylinder arch profile extruded along one axis, painted in a teal-grey metal tone, with corrugation suggested through paint striping instead of extra geometry. I'm also planning details like a front door with frame, a small porch/steps, and a glowing window for each hut.

For the glowing window, I'm thinking of using an SVG texture with cross mullions, a warm gradient, and maybe a lamp silhouette for coziness. I'm also adding a stovepipe chimney with cheap smoke puffs made from a few scaled icosahedron spheres in pale peach, a lantern by the door with a glow sphere and bracket, and a wooden sign board with rendered text like "POLAR STATION 7 · WEATHER & ICE" done via an SVG texture on a box face.

For the flag, I'll use a thin textured box instead of a plane to avoid single-sided rendering issues. I'm also planning a lab module quonset hut connected to the main hut by a small corridor box, plus a lattice radio mast with tapered legs, cross bracing, guy wires, and a red aircraft light glowing at the top.

Now I'm adding a satellite dish (lathe-geometry cap on a tilted mount with feed horn) near the lab roof, a Stevenson screen weather box, a rotating-cup anemometer on the hut roof, a small wind turbine with three blades, and a tilted solar panel array with grid texturing. I'm also placing a snowmobile with a lofted body and ski runners nearby.

I'm sketching more scene elements: the snowmobile gets a tracked rear end, handlebars, windshield, and headlight glow, plus a trailing sled loaded with crates. I'm also planning fuel drums with color bands, a stack of supply crates under a tarp, a rack of ice-core sample tubes, and a tripod ice-drill rig positioned near a drilled hole, while being careful to space everything out so nothing overlaps.

For finishing touches, I'm adding footprint trails as flat darkened snow decals leading from the hut door to the lab and snowmobile, plus a small researcher figure in an orange parka with a furry hood standing by the Stevenson screen holding a clipboard for character, maybe alongside a sled dog if the part budget allows -- keeping a rough target of around 900 lines and writing compact helper functions to stay efficient.

I'm also scattering sparse snow-dusted conifers in the dark background for depth, a few snow-capped boulders, and painting subtle color variation into the snow itself -- pale lavender-white highlights with warm undertones on top and pinkish drifts on the sides. For a Firewatch-style lighting effect, I want to fake long cast shadows stretching toward the viewer from the hut and other structures using flat blue-tinted quads just above the snow surface.

Working out the shadow geometry now -- thin extruded slabs sitting barely above the snow layer (positioned so they peek just above the surface without clipping into the bevel), oriented based on where the sun is implied to be. I'm settling on a purple-blue tone like "#8d86bd" for the shadow color to match that painterly Firewatch look.

Setting up the module imports now, pulling in the builder utilities, noise/paint/mix helpers, and the glow kit, then starting to configure the builder instance.

Given the scene's size, I'll set paintSize to 2048 since the surfaces are large and flat-styled, which keeps texel density reasonable while staying under the atlas limit. For colors, I'm defining a palette of consts, aiming to stay around 40 distinct flat colors well under the 64-color cap.

Defining more color constants...

Still tuning shading logic...

I'm thinking I should factor out a reusable tone-lighting helper function that both the main surface paint and the siding paint can call, so lighting calculations stay consistent across materials rather than duplicating the math.

Since paints can nest and return other paints, I can build siding as a paint that picks between a dark-groove tone paint and a base tone paint depending on position, applying a periodic line pattern along the y-axis that works uniformly across the gable walls despite their differing normals. I also want to think through whether to add snow accumulation near the wall base, though a stilted hut design might make that unnecessary.

Now I'm working out a rounded-rectangle outline generator for the terrain base, computing corner points at quarter-circle intervals with optional wobble offsets so the footprint reads as a naturally uneven rounded shape when extruded.

Still working out the perimeter point order...

I'm thinking the wobble should apply only to the snow layer's outline, giving it an overhanging drip look over the ice and rock layers beneath, so I'll size rock slightly smaller, ice stepped in, and snow slightly larger with wobble. I'll also apply a bit of corner smoothing to the snow outline to keep it organic rather than sharp.

For the front faces, I'm planning to paint horizontal purple strata bands with noise on the rock layer, a blue gradient with highlights on the ice, and a snowy drip-textured tone on the snow sides. I also want to scatter ellipsoid snow drifts near hut bases and edges using scaled sphere geometries.

Now I'm setting up helper functions for buildings — a `box` helper for creating positioned box geometries, a `boxOn` variant for placing boxes on a base, and a `cyl` helper for cylinders, all taking dimensions, color, and placement options.

For the first hut, I'm planning its layout: centered at a specific point with set width, depth, wall height, and roof height, raised on stilts above the snow. I'm working out the stilt posts, skid beams, and floor slab dimensions before moving into the main body structure.

Now I'm extruding the body as a pentagon profile (walls plus gable roof shape) along the depth axis, painted as siding, which naturally creates the triangular gable ends. Then I'm calculating the roof slope angle and panel lengths, including overhang, and positioning each roof panel along the slope from eave to ridge with proper offsets.

Working out the panel placement and rotation geometry...

Adding snow clumps at the eaves with small flattened spheres, plus dark wood fascia boards along the gable slopes. Now I'm planning the front door placement and dimensions with a teal-colored door and lighter frame.

Adding a porch with step boxes, a deck slab, a small tilted canopy roof over the door, and a hanging lantern for glow. Working out window placement on the front face with wood frames, sills, and shutters, plus a small round porthole window on the gable end.

I'm reconsidering the roof orientation — rather than having the gable ends face the viewer, I want the ridge running along the long axis so the sloped roof faces present over the front door wall, which means reworking the extrusion profile and axis of extrusion accordingly.

Writing roof panel rotation math...

I verify the normal vectors are perpendicular to each roof slope's direction with correct orientation for front and back, then plan a generic roofSlope helper and a gableHut function to generate the key frame positions, with other shapes like a quonset hut and maybe a smaller shed in mind too.

Now I'm placing the hut's details: a front door and porch deck positioned along the z+ wall, and a stovepipe chimney positioned off-center, computing its base height from the roof surface profile at that offset so it sits correctly below the ridge.

I'm adding rising smoke puffs using small faceted icosahedra that increase in size and drift sideways to suggest wind, tinted in soft dusty pink tones, plus an anemometer mounted on a mast on the hut roof with a pole, cross-arms, three cups, and a wind vane.

Now I'm working out the quonset-style lab hut geometry: positioning it near the main hut, orienting its arched cross-section along one axis while extruding length along the other, setting wall height, radius, and vertical placement on its skids, and figuring out where a connecting door or corridor would sit relative to the main hut's position.

I'll raise the straight wall to 0.16 with a radius 0.2 arch on top, putting the glowing portholes on that vertical wall facing outward, then work out the arch outline points by stepping angle from 0 to 180 degrees to trace the semicircular roof profile.

Now I'm defining the corrugated paint pattern using periodic stripes along the length axis to create darker lines at regular intervals.

I need to exclude the end caps from the stripe pattern since a constant x-value there would color the whole face uniformly instead of striping it, so I'm restricting the effect to surfaces where the normal isn't mostly along x. For the roof, I'm adding partial snow coverage by thresholding the surface normal's y-component against a noisy edge so upward-facing arch surfaces get a mix of teal and snow with a hand-drawn wobble rather than a hard line.

Since the arch is faceted in 20° steps, I'm picking a threshold around 0.8 so roughly the top couple of facets on each side get snow, relying on the interpolated normals to keep the painting smooth. I'm also considering adding a door with a frame on the near end wall, plus small exterior details like roof vents or a radome to break up the silhouette.

For the radome, I'll add a satellite dish on the lab roof, mounted on a cylinder tilted toward the sky, built as a lathed parabolic shell — tracing a profile curve outward from the center with a slight depth so it looks concave.

I'm adding a feed horn rod extending along the dish axis with a small cone tip. For placement, I'll go with one large ground-mounted dish on a tripod near the mast, while the lab roof gets vents, a whip antenna, and an anemometer instead of a second dish, and I'm positioning the radio mast off to the side.

Now I'm building out the mast's tripod legs with tapering radius, cross-bracing bands in alternating red and white, a glowing light sphere with whip on top, and guy wires running from mid-height down to ground stakes, keeping the rod geometry simple with fewer sides for performance.

I'm also planning a separate wind turbine positioned away from the mast, with a tapered white tower, nacelle box, hub cone, and three extruded blades set at a rest angle, working out how to orient each blade's cross-section so it faces the viewer correctly while rotating around the hub.

Adding three solar panels at a tilted angle, computing rotation so their normals face up and forward, with dark blue frames and grid lines painted via UV coordinates.

Now I'm laying out the base scene: the hut sits off-center with its porch facing the viewer, the lab module sits to the right connected by a short corridor, and I'm positioning the mast, turbine, and large dish around the edges to balance the composition.

I'm placing a three-panel solar array near the back, adding a Stevenson screen with a researcher nearby, and sketching a snowmobile angled toward the viewer with a sled of crates behind it, plus fuel drums off to the side for extra ground detail.

I'm also working out the ice drill tripod's placement relative to the researcher, laying a trodden footpath connecting the porch, Stevenson screen, snowmobile, and lab, and dotting spruce trees along the left and right rear edges to frame the scene.

Now I'm placing the wind mast and turbine tower along the ridge behind the lab, checking tree clearance around the mast legs, then scattering a few rocks near the solar panel for natural variation.

I'm deciding whether to add a husky by the sled or keep the scene to just the researcher to stay within the parts budget. For textures, I'm settling on a core set: window glow, sign, flag emblem, aurora, a crate stencil reading something like "ICE CORE," a hazard label on the drums, and a thermometer marking on the researcher character.

Designing window texture SVG...

Now I'm thinking through a wooden sign reading "STATION 7" and "ARCTIC RESEARCH" for the research hut, with a cream-colored plank background and bold lettering, trying to figure out where to mount it on posts near the entrance.

I'm finalizing scene placements -- positioning the snowmobile, flagpole with a flag blowing in the wind, Stevenson screen, and sign so nothing overlaps near the lab corridor, then adding small glowing accents like window panes, a lantern, mast light, and headlight.

For the snowmobile, I'm working out a way to build it in local coordinates and rotate it as a group using a yaw transform, so I need a helper function that converts local positions to world positions and applies a combined yaw and local rotation to each part.

I confirm `b.part` accepts a `quat` field and colors can take Paint values, with DEG defined as a local constant. I'll use the rig helper for most objects with simple yaw rotations, and since `b` is scoped inside build(), I'll just define these helper functions within build() itself rather than passing `b` around.

Setting up module-level imports and constants...

Still blending lighting colors...

Now I'm sketching a siding paint function that creates grooved horizontal board lines by alternating a base and groove color based on periodic Y position, while checking that roof panels properly cover the gable triangle along the ridge.

For snow coloring, I'm defining a base/shadow palette and planning to add mottled color variation across the ground using noise, mixing in subtle pink/blue tints where the noise value crosses a threshold.

For the rock face, I'm sketching out a layered strata scheme by height, assigning darker purples near the base and lighter tones higher up, with a bit of noise wobble so the bands aren't perfectly flat.

Adding ice gradient and sky color stops...

Still writing ridge shading logic...

Still defining ridge layers...

I'm adjusting the base size to 1.22 and shifting the panel centre back to -1.20 so its front sits at -1.18, then recalculating the sun, halo, aurora, and ridge positions to stack cleanly in front of it with small depth gaps to avoid z-fighting.

For the aurora texture, since alpha cutoff would clip partial transparency, I need to use only opaque fills and build the fading effect by layering multiple solid shapes instead of relying on gradient transparency.

Writing aurora shape code...

For stars, I'm scattering small octahedron glyphs across the upper sky region with randomized positions, giving them a soft warm glow to suggest twinkling starlight behind the aurora.

Now I'm placing the sun as a glowing circle near the ridge line, partially obscured, surrounded by a soft colored halo, then moving on to building layered conical shapes for the spruce trees.

For snow caps, I'm scaling smaller cones matching the same slope positioned near each tier's apex, slightly enlarged to avoid z-fighting so the white snow appears to dust only the upper portion of each tier.

I'm sizing the trunk as a dark cylinder and defining the four tiers with specific radii, heights, and base positions scaled per tree, using faceted cone geometry for a low-poly look. Now I'm starting to think through rock placement.

For rocks, I'm using irregular icosahedron shapes with rotation and dark purple coloring, plus a flattened icosahedron cap for snow sitting slightly above center. Then I move on to the Stevenson screen weather box, planning the legs, louvered white body, flat slanted roof, and a thermometer detail sticking out.

Now I'm working out the researcher figure's placement and scale relative to the hut — using the wall height of 0.30 units as 2.4m real-world to derive a scale factor, making the person about 0.22 units tall for a 1.75m figure, and sizing the door opening proportionally at roughly 0.24-0.25 of the wall height.

I'm checking proportions for the rest of the scene too: snowmobile, mast, mine shed, drums, Stevenson screen, solar panels, and hut footprint all scale consistently against this factor. Now I'm sketching how to build the researcher model with capsule sweeps for limbs, dark pants and boots, and an orange parka torso shape.

Fleshing out the parka with tapered hips-to-shoulders geometry, a fur-trimmed hood with a small skin-toned face sphere, teal scarf, backpack box, and arms as capsules — one holding a clipboard, the other pointing with a pencil.

For the capsule limbs I'm confirming the builder's signature takes world-space endpoints, a radius (or tapered radii pair), and color right after the radius, with optional settings like sides for the cross-section. Writing the stripe paint function...

Positioning the snowmobile at roughly (-0.8, ground, 0.62) with a yaw around -35° so it faces toward the viewer's left-front, leaving the sled trailing toward the back-right. Now I'm adding fuel drums as small cylinders, placing three of them near the left end of the hut.

For the crates, I'm planning a stack of three wooden boxes with a UV-based paint function that darkens the border pixels to simulate cross-slat edges and wood siding detail.

For the ice fishing setup, I'm sketching a tripod drill rig with a spiral-striped auger tube descending into a dark blue ice hole ringed in bright blue, plus a wood tray holding several pale blue ice core cylinders lined up beside the drill.

Now I'm adding a footprint trail: small flattened oval prints alternating left and right along a sampled path curve from the porch toward the Stevenson screen and drill, each print a short scaled cylinder tinted shadowy purple-gray, with separate trails connecting the porch to the lab door.

I also want parallel snowmobile tread marks behind the sled -- thin dark extruded polyline slabs swept along a path with a box section, keeping the frame orientation upright so the tread sits flat on the ground.

Working out the geometry for the corridor connecting the hut and lab, calculating wall positions, porthole heights, and the arch structure so the dimensions line up correctly between the two sections.

Still building the lattice...
